RocKIT supports the management of research data throughout its lifecycle. It helps users enrich research data with metadata that makes it easier to find, understand, and process, upload it to data repositories, and continue curating it after publication. This guide introduces the workflows and tools available for these tasks.
RocKIT includes a native agent chat interface for AI-assisted RO-Crate work. The assistant is prompted to act as an RO-Crate data steward and to prefer RO-Crate MCP tools for metadata edits.

RocKIT watches the open workspace's ro-crate-metadata.json file. When an AI client, MCP tool, or other external program modifies that file, RocKIT rereads it after a short delay, compares it with the loaded state, and starts the review workflow. Saves made by RocKIT itself are not treated as external changes.
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. An MCP server is a local service that exposes RocKIT tools to an AI client in a standard way, including reading, validating, and editing RO-Crate metadata.

Multi-entity editing is for applying the same metadata change to several selected entities. It is most useful for files or datasets that share a creator, licence, subject, project, or other repeated property.
Use the Metadata Editor interface to edit the data of a single entity.

The structure of an RO-Crate is determined by the references between the entities involved. Entities therefore form a structure not merely through their locations in the file system: their relationships are described by properties recorded in the RO-Crate metadata.

RocKIT keeps an in-memory history of RO-Crate metadata changes during the current application session. Supported editor, structure, delete, conversion, and bulk-edit operations are applied through that history service so they can participate in undo and redo.
Open Validation Errors from the RO-Crate menu to inspect problems found in the current crate. The Structure panel and Entities panel also mark entities that have validation errors.
RocKIT runs as a desktop application. Always use the latest installer or application package for your operating system.

RocKIT uses the standard Theia workbench layout with RO-Crate-specific panels. The main working areas are:

The Entities panel lists RO-Crate entities independently of the file tree. It is useful for people, organizations, URLs, schema-defined objects, and any entity that is hard to find through the dataset hierarchy.

The Metadata Profile Manager stores metadata profiles that can be associated with RO-Crate entities. Profiles define which metadata fields appear when editing a dataset, file, or other RO-Crate entity, which fields are required, and what kind of values can be entered. Examples include profiles based on the Harvard Dataverse metadata blocks and described in the ARP CEDAR repository; these profiles can be used to describe datasets and data entities.
RO-Crate Preview opens a dialog showing the RO-Crate JSON currently held in RocKIT application state. It is useful for reviewing exactly what the editor will save.
The Metadata Editor is the form-based editor for one selected entity. It edits the RO-Crate JSON through structured fields instead of requiring manual JSON editing.
The RO-Crate menu groups the main RocKIT views and tools.

The RO-Crate Structure Panel shows the crate as a dataset and file tree. It is the best view for understanding what the root dataset contains and how nested datasets and files are connected. Open the panel with the Structure Panel command in the RO-Crate menu.

Eclipse Theia is an open-source framework: a shared foundation for applications with different purposes. RocKIT uses this foundation for its workspace and adds tools for managing RO-Crate data packages and research metadata. For a data steward, Theia mainly helps bring files, the structure of a data package, and metadata together in one manageable interface.

The Workspace panel is Theia's standard file explorer for the open folder. It shows physical files and folders from the root of the data package opened for editing. In contrast, the RO-Crate Structure Panel, RO-Crate Editor, and Entities Panel show metadata entities loaded from ro-crate-metadata.json: the metadata description and the physical files in an RO-Crate data package may differ.

The Data Repository Manager stores connection settings for remote repositories used by repository-oriented workflows. RocKIT recognizes ARP Data Repository, generic Dataverse repositories, and Zenodo; the ARP Data Repository workflow has the most complete support.
Saving and exporting are separate actions.

Remote-to-local conversion is for ARP Data Repository RO-Crates whose file and dataset entities use ARP remote identifiers such as https://w3id.org/arp/ro-id/.../file/.... Local editing and export are easier when those entities use workspace-relative paths.

RocKIT can import RO-Crate workspaces from remote repositories, export new datasets, and link, update, or synchronize local and remote copies. These operations are not available directly from the File menu. Open RO-Crate > Repository Operations to display the Select Data Repository window.
Start with a clean folder structure. Rename files and organize folders before creating final metadata so entity identifiers can stay stable.

RocKIT commands are available from menus and the Theia Command Palette. Open the palette from View > Command Palette… or with its keyboard shortcut. See RO-Crate Menu Reference for the structure of the RO-Crate menu.
ro-crate-metadata.json is the primary RO-Crate metadata file. RocKIT loads it from the workspace root and saves edited metadata back to it.

From local files to a research dataset. Organize, describe, validate, review and package. Publish when you are ready. Organize — Open a folder or an existing RO-Crate. Work with files on your machine. Describe — Add FAIR metadata freely, or follow a profile for your research domain. Validate & review — Check requirements and inspect the metadata before sharing. Package — Export your dataset as an RO-Crate ZIP, with data and metadata together. Publish — Choose a repository. Deposit or update through supported integrations. Your entire workflow in RocKIT. RocKIT supports every step, from local files to publishing your research dataset.

Describe it your way. Choose fields from available schemas. Import profiles to guide metadata editing and validation for your research dataset. Choose schema elements: Use the terms your dataset needs. Import a profile: Follow its required fields and rules. Edit & validate: Complete and check your metadata. RocKIT imports CEDAR templates from the ARP Schema Registry. You can also add individual fields from schema vocabularies such as Schema.org.

Prepare locally. Share when ready. Keep authoring local, package your RO-Crate, or use a supported repository to deposit and maintain your dataset. Bring a dataset in: Import a remote dataset as a local RO-Crate. Work on your computer: Edit descriptions, review files and validate metadata. Send a reviewed package: Create or update a deposit in your chosen repository. One package, two parts. Your research files and their linked metadata travel together in an RO-Crate ZIP.

Less repetition. You stay in control. Use Codex, Claude or OpenCode. RocKIT provides an RO-Crate MCP server with tools to author and validate RO-Crates. Available agent tools include web search, file extraction, image understanding, browser use, computer use and RO-Crate authoring and validation through MCP. Your agent works with a RocKIT dataset—local files and FAIR metadata. You choose the task and stay in control: review, reject or fix the agent's work.

RocKIT supports the management of research data throughout its lifecycle. It helps users enrich research data with metadata that makes it easier to find, understand, and process, upload it to data repositories, and continue curating it after publication. This guide introduces the workflows and tools available for these tasks. RocKIT is a desktop application; see Installation and Startup for instructions on installing and launching it. To begin using RocKIT, follow one of the introductory guides in Getting Started: create a new RO-Crate, open and edit an existing RO-Crate, or import a dataset from a remote repository. Important: RocKIT may create new files and directories inside the directory opened as a workspace for editing research data. These can include the ro-crate-metadata.json metadata file, the ro-crate-preview.html preview, and the .rockit directory used to store data required by RocKIT. RocKIT's interface is available in multiple languages. The documentation introduces RocKIT concepts in the language selected for the documentation. A description of the main working areas and the application's structure is available on the Application Layout page. For common use cases and guides covering complete processes, see End-to-End Workflows. General RO-Crate background is covered in the RO-Crate Quickstart in the AROMA documentation. This guide concentrates on how those concepts are represented in the RocKIT interface and workflows.

RocKIT includes a native agent chat interface for AI-assisted RO-Crate work. The assistant is prompted to act as an RO-Crate data steward and to prefer RO-Crate MCP tools for metadata edits. The chat panel can start a new session for the current workspace, resume previous sessions, delete individual chat sessions, or clear saved chat history for the workspace. Use the transcript copy action when you need to share the conversation or keep an audit trail. Messages sent to the assistant include useful workspace context, including the currently selected RO-Crate entity and validation errors. The assistant may propose metadata changes, run available tools, or help interpret validation and repository workflow results. When an AI client or external program modifies ro-crate-metadata.json directly, RocKIT detects and handles the changes through a separate review workflow. See Reviewing external RO-Crate changes for the details.

Agent workflows depend on the configured RO-Crate MCP server and the installed native agent provider. If the assistant cannot connect, check the MCP daemon startup, provider credentials, and workspace permissions. The first time you start a supported AI client from the RO-Crate menu, RocKIT checks whether that client's user configuration already contains the rocrate MCP server. This is required so the external client can use the same RO-Crate MCP tools as RocKIT and make metadata changes against the current workspace. If the entry is missing, RocKIT asks for confirmation and then adds the configuration. The entry contains the Node/Electron runtime resolved by RocKIT, the RO-Crate MCP server path, the connection socket, and the ROCRATE_MCP_DEFAULT_MODE=local environment setting. The configuration is created or updated at user level, so RocKIT does not ask again on later launches when the same rocrate MCP entry is already present. The target file depends on the client: ~/.codex/config.toml for Codex, the user-level Claude MCP configuration for Claude, ~/.config/opencode/config.json for Opencode, ~/.kilo/config.json for Kilo, ~/.roo/config.json for Roo, ~/.gemini/settings.json for Gemini, and ~/.qwen/settings.json for Qwen. The current RO-Crate menu supports these AI clients: Codex, Claude, Opencode, Kilo, Roo, Gemini, and Qwen. The built-in RocKIT chat panel is available for Codex and Claude; the other clients are launched as external terminal tools. RocKIT only shows menu entries for clients where it can find the command-line executable or a known user configuration directory for that client.

When an AI-assisted Dataverse upload returns an updated RO-Crate with assigned dataset or file IDs, RocKIT can prompt you to replace the local ro-crate-metadata.json with the Dataverse-updated version. Accept only after reviewing the dataset PID, repository URL, and expected upload result. AI assistance should not replace human review. Before accepting or saving generated changes, preview the crate, validate it, and inspect changed entities that affect publication, authorship, licensing, or repository upload.

RocKIT watches the open workspace's ro-crate-metadata.json file. When an AI client, MCP tool, or other external program modifies that file, RocKIT rereads it after a short delay, compares it with the loaded state, and starts the review workflow. Saves made by RocKIT itself are not treated as external changes.

The default behavior is to ask before reloading. RocKIT reports that ro-crate-metadata.json changed outside the application and offers three choices: Reload: load the new version from disk. Always Reload: load the new version and switch the user preference to automatic reload. Ignore: keep the version currently loaded in RocKIT and write it back to disk. The behavior is controlled by the rockit.roCrate.externalChangeAction preference. Supported values are: prompt: ask before reloading. auto: automatically load external changes. off: do not start an automatic reload or review workflow for external changes. If the external change leaves invalid JSON on disk, RocKIT does not load it. When a last valid in-memory RO-Crate is available, RocKIT offers to restore that version. If ro-crate-metadata.json is missing, RocKIT removes the related approval state, clears the loaded RO-Crate, and offers a recovery path.

When the external version is reloaded, RocKIT collects field-level differences between the previous RO-Crate and the new ro-crate-metadata.json. The comparison covers root-level properties and properties on entities in @graph. Each difference becomes an approval item. The item records the affected entity, property name, operation (create, update, or delete), previous value when needed, timestamp, and whether the change has been approved. New or changed items are not approved by default.

The RO-Crate editor presents approval items as changes proposed by AI or an external tool. For each affected field, the user can decide to: accept the suggestion when the externally written value is correct; reject the suggestion when the previous value should be kept or restored; manually edit the value when the suggestion is useful but needs correction. These decisions are also recorded in RocKIT's history. Accepting a suggestion is labeled Accept AI suggestion, rejecting one is labeled Reject AI suggestion, and manual correction is labeled Edit AI suggestion. Reject and manual-edit actions are merged with the related metadata change in history, so the decision and the actual RO-Crate edit can be handled as one operation.

After working with AI or an external agent, always review the pending fields, then validate the crate and check the preview before saving. When automatic reload is enabled, reviewing the approval markers is especially important because the version on disk is loaded into RocKIT without a separate human confirmation step.

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. An MCP server is a local service that exposes RocKIT tools to an AI client in a standard way, including reading, validating, and editing RO-Crate metadata. The daemon is the background-running instance of that same server: RocKIT starts or reuses it, and clients connect to it through a local socket. It is therefore not a separate user interface, but a tool bridge between the AI client and RocKIT.

When the RocKIT MCP server starts successfully, its telemetry and statistics dashboard can be opened in a browser. By default it is available at http://127.0.0.1:9393. The host and port can be changed with the ROCRATE_DASHBOARD_HOST and ROCRATE_DASHBOARD_PORT environment variables, and the dashboard can be disabled with ROCRATE_DASHBOARD_ENABLED=false. The dashboard shows sessions, tool calls, errors, timings, and external dependency usage, so it is useful for troubleshooting and reviewing AI-assisted workflows.

The AI client learns about RocKIT operations through the standard MCP tool discovery mechanism. When the client starts or connects to the rocrate MCP server, it requests the list of available tools. For each operation, the server provides the tool name, description, input schema, required parameters, and constraints. The client then makes this tool list available to the model. The model decides, based on the user request, system and workflow instructions, and tool descriptions, whether a task can be answered in text or requires an MCP tool call. For example, a validation request may use validate_crate, a metadata edit may use apply_changes or write_crate_atomic, and a request to inspect the crate may use read_crate. RocKIT also supports this decision with agent workflow guidance: the assistant instructions ask the client to read the workflow documents before RO-Crate work and to prefer RO-Crate MCP tools for metadata edits. The exact timing and selection of tool calls is still determined by the tool-calling logic of the specific AI client and model.

Dataverse workflows: upload_rocrate_to_dataverse, adopt_pending_dataverse_rocrate, download_rocrate_from_dataverse. Ontology and schema suggestions: list_schema_registry, register_schema, list_types, suggest_types, get_type_details, list_properties_for_type, suggest_properties, get_property_details.

Operation Description set_agent_session_context Sets the agent session launch context. Agents launched from RocKIT use it to report that they are running inside the application. read_agent_workflow_doc Reads RO-Crate agent workflow guidance bundled with the MCP server. By default it returns the main rocrate_workflow.md document. open_aroma_for_local_file Registers a local ro-crate-metadata.json file with the local bridge and returns an AROMA URL that can read, save, and auto-refresh that file. search Runs a web search through Tavily. It requires TAVILY_API_KEY on the server or an API key passed with the call. download_url Downloads one URL. With raw_html=true it returns the raw HTML source; otherwise it returns extracted readable text. read_crate Reads and returns RO-Crate JSON. Local mode reads from disk; remote mode uses the crate payload provided in the call. create_default_rocrate Creates an initial ro-crate-metadata.json for a directory that does not yet have an RO-Crate. It scans files, prepares the ignore file, and writes metadata atomically. apply_changes Applies a compact change set to a crate. In local mode it persists changes by default; with dryRun=true it previews the result without writing. update_profile_conforms_to Updates conformsTo profile URLs on one Dataset or File entity, defaulting to the root dataset, using add, remove, or set operations. validate_crate Validates crate structure and references, including active profile conformance checks and value-set errors or hints. write_crate_atomic Atomically writes crate JSON to disk, running profile validation and, by default, automatic context reconciliation before writing. get_rocrate_context Returns crate context and profile hints. It detects conformsTo profile URLs and emits profile resolution guidance. suggest_context_terms Suggests mergeContext mappings for terms used in @graph but not declared in @context and not known from the default RO-Crate context. resolve_metadata_profile Resolves a profile URL through the metadata-profile-index and returns related profile records and converted profile file paths. prepare_remote_profile_payload Builds a schemaIndex and profileContents payload from local profile mappings so remote-mode profile-aware tools can use it. create_profile_context Creates a server-side cached profile context and returns a profileContextId for later remote profile-aware calls. get_profile_context_info Returns a metadata summary for a cached profileContextId without returning full profile contents. delete_profile_context Deletes a cached profileContextId from server memory. list_remote_templates Browses or searches configured CEDAR registry providers for remote CEDAR templates. list_remote_template_tree Browses configured CEDAR providers as a folder tree and lists only unimported template leaves for profile selection. import_remote_template Imports a remote CEDAR template by name, template URL, or conformsTo value into the shared metadata profile store. list_metadata_profiles Lists persisted CEDAR or Recrate metadata profiles from the shared metadata-profile-index.json store. import_metadata_profile Imports a CEDAR metadata profile from a direct URL or local source path into the shared profile store. delete_metadata_profile Deletes one persisted CEDAR or Recrate metadata profile and its source and converted files. The operation requires explicit destructive confirmation. upload_rocrate_to_dataverse Uploads an RO-Crate to the Dataverse ARP API. For a new dataset it sends a ZIP with metadata and referenced files; for an existing PID it sends a JSON metadata update. adopt_pending_dataverse_rocrate Replaces the local metadata with a Dataverse-updated pending RO-Crate returned by upload_rocrate_to_dataverse. download_rocrate_from_dataverse Downloads crate JSON from the Dataverse ARP API by PID. In local mode, it only persists to disk when write=true. list_schema_registry Lists persisted ontology schema registry entries used by ontology query tools. register_schema Registers or updates one ontology schema source in the persisted schema registry. list_types Lists distilled ontology class or type candidates available from the shared context and schema catalog. suggest_types Suggests matching ontology types for a free-text query using shared catalog ranking. get_type_details Returns details for one ontology type, such as label, comment, parent types, and property count. list_properties_for_type Lists properties for a given type, optionally including inherited properties. suggest_properties Suggests matching properties for a free-text query constrained by one or more type IDs. get_property_details Returns details for one ontology property, such as label, comment, domain, and range.
Open a prepared folder, generate ro-crate-metadata.json when prompted, describe the root dataset, drag missing files into the Structure panel, save, validate, preview, and export.

Open the root dataset ./ in the RO-Crate Editor. Add title or name, description, creators, organizations, licence, dates, keywords, related publications, and repository-required fields. Reuse existing Person and Organization entities where possible.
Import the profile in Metadata Profile Manager, then associate it with the target entity from the editor or profile selector. Fill the new fields and validate.
Copy the file into the workspace, drag it into the target dataset in the Structure panel, open the new File entity, add descriptive metadata, then save and validate.

Create or add a folder, represent it as a Dataset entity, and connect it to its parent dataset with hasPart. Add files under that nested dataset and describe the nested dataset if it has its own meaning.
Save the crate, run validation, preview the JSON, then use clean export. Open the ZIP and verify that required files and ro-crate-metadata.json are present.
Open the folder, let RocKIT load or repair the metadata, validate, inspect the Structure and Entities panels, and save only after you understand any conversion or repair changes.

Multi-entity editing is for applying the same metadata change to several selected entities. It is most useful for files or datasets that share a creator, licence, subject, project, or other repeated property. Select multiple entities in the Structure panel or Entities panel, then open the edit action from the context menu or available command. RocKIT determines which selected entities can be edited together and shows the properties that make sense for the selection.

Selected entities: the top of the dialog shows the number of entities to be edited. Open the entity list to verify by name and type that the selection contains the intended items. Select profiles: determines which profile properties are available. When necessary, RocKIT also assigns the selected profiles to the edited entities. Enable properties from other ontologies: makes supported properties from additional ontologies available alongside the fields defined by the profiles. Edit operations: each numbered row describes one change to be performed on every selected entity. Property selects the metadata field, Operator selects how it will be changed, and the final field supplies the new or affected value. The value editor adapts to the selected property, for example as a text, date, number, or entity field. Operators: Add preserves existing values and adds a new one; Remove removes only the specified value; Set replaces the complete value of the property; and Unset removes the property and therefore requires no value. Add rule and the trash icon: creates another operation row or removes the corresponding row. Operations run in the displayed order. Start multi-edit: is enabled only when the setup is complete and valid. It applies every listed operation to all selected entities. Close dismisses the dialog without applying changes. Bulk edits are recorded as RO-Crate history changes, so supported changes can be undone during the same session. After a bulk edit, validate the crate and spot-check several affected entities in the normal editor.
Use the Metadata Editor interface to edit the data of a single entity.

The structure of an RO-Crate is determined by the references between the entities involved. Entities therefore form a structure not merely through their locations in the file system: their relationships are described by properties recorded in the RO-Crate metadata. The natural hierarchical structure is normally defined by hasPart relations. These express which additional entities are contained by a dataset or another composite entity. The interface for viewing and managing this structure is described on the RO-Crate Structure page.

RocKIT keeps an in-memory history of RO-Crate metadata changes during the current application session. Supported editor, structure, delete, conversion, and bulk-edit operations are applied through that history service so they can participate in undo and redo. Use the standard Undo and Redo commands while an RO-Crate editor or RO-Crate panel is active. A single user action may be stored as one grouped change even if it updates several JSON references. Undo and redo are intended for metadata state, not as a full file-system rollback system. They should not be treated as a substitute for backups or version control. External file edits, manual changes to ro-crate-metadata.json, and operating-system file moves may not be reversible through RocKIT history. If you make a mistake: Try Undo immediately. If the crate has not been saved, close without saving or reload the workspace if appropriate. If the crate was saved, restore a previous copy of ro-crate-metadata.json from backup or version control. Validate after recovery. Some development builds include an AppState debug panel. It is useful for diagnosing state problems, but it is not required for normal editing.

Open Validation Errors from the RO-Crate menu to inspect problems found in the current crate. The Structure panel and Entities panel also mark entities that have validation errors. Validation messages usually identify an entity and a property or profile rule. Clicking an entry in the error list navigates directly to the invalid element. Correct the field in the Metadata Editor, then refresh validation or save and re-run the relevant workflow. Common causes include: Missing required fields. Invalid URLs, dates, numbers, or controlled values. References to entities that do not exist in @graph. File or dataset entities that are no longer connected through hasPart. Missing profiles referenced by conformsTo. Metadata that does not match the selected profile. Validation is especially important before export. The preview shows the current JSON, but validation tells you whether that JSON satisfies the rules RocKIT can check. If a validation error remains after you believe it is fixed, save the crate, reopen the entity, and verify that the value is stored in the expected property and entity. Some errors are caused by a related entity rather than the entity currently visible in the editor.
RocKIT runs as a desktop application. Always use the latest installer or application package for your operating system.

On Windows, download and run the latest RocKIT - RO-Crate Kit Setup *.exe installer. The installer runs automatically, creates a desktop shortcut, and RocKIT can then be started from the shortcut or from the Windows application menu. The installed application can be large, so check that enough free disk space is available before installation.

On Linux, the AppImage package is the simplest option because it does not require installation. Download the latest RocKIT - RO-Crate Kit-*.AppImage file, then run the following commands in the directory where you downloaded it: chmod +x ./RocKIT*.AppImage ./RocKIT*.AppImage If the AppImage does not start because FUSE support is missing, install the required package on Ubuntu and Linux Mint based systems: sudo apt update sudo apt install -y libfuse2 Then run the AppImage file again. Alternatively, you can install the latest .deb package: sudo apt install ./RocKIT*.deb After installing the .deb package, RocKIT can be started from the application menu as RocKIT - RO-Crate Kit, or from the command line with the command provided by the application package. On Linux Mint and Ubuntu based systems, the AppImage package is recommended. Choose the .deb package if you want to use RocKIT as an installed application.
On macOS, download and open the latest RocKIT - RO-Crate Kit-*.dmg file. Drag RocKIT.app to the Applications folder, or to the folder where you want to keep the application.

To install a new version, you usually do not need to remove the previous version first. Download the new installer or application package for your operating system, then install it over the existing version. On Windows, run the new .exe installer and follow the installer steps. On macOS, open the new .dmg file, then drag the application to the Applications folder. If the system asks, choose to replace the existing application. On Linux, install the new package in the usual way when using a .deb package. When using AppImage, replace the earlier AppImage file with the new version. After updating, restart the application. Existing settings and workspace files are normally preserved.

RocKIT's interface is available in multiple languages. Choose the display language from File > Preferences > Configure Display Language. On first startup, RocKIT automatically creates the default ARP Production CEDAR profile provider. You can review or modify it in Metadata Profile Manager, available from RO-Crate > Metadata Profile Manager; open the provider list with the Configure Providers icon. For repository export, you can configure an ARP Dataverse, generic Dataverse, or Zenodo repository in Data Repository Manager. ARP Dataverse is RocKIT's main supported repository platform; for that setup, open RO-Crate > Data Repository Manager, then use + Add Repository to enter the connection details for the data repository. Recommended values: Field Value Name Any display name. Base URL https://repo.researchdata.hu API Token The user's API token generated in the repository interface.

When the application opens, RocKIT shows a splash screen while the workbench starts. After startup, the main application window appears. If no folder is open yet, the workspace is empty and the RO-Crate panels have no crate content to display. From this point you normally choose one of three starting paths: Create a new RO-Crate from a folder of files. See Quick Start: Create an RO-Crate from Scratch. Open and continue editing an existing RO-Crate. See Quick Start: Open and Edit an Existing RO-Crate. Import a dataset from a remote repository. See Quick Start: Import a Dataset from a Remote Repository. Use File > Open Folder or the equivalent Theia workspace command to choose the folder you want to work with. Once a folder is open, RocKIT initializes the RO-Crate views for that workspace. Depending on the folder contents, it may load an existing crate or offer options for creating one. If you close the workspace or start the application without opening a folder, you can still use the menus and workbench, but there is no active RO-Crate to edit until you open a workspace folder.

When creating a new RO-Crate, the main task is not simply packaging files. The goal is to describe the research data in the folder with clear, checkable metadata. RocKIT creates the ro-crate-metadata.json file and then helps you describe the root dataset, files, and related contextual entities. Prepare a folder that contains the files you want to package. Choose File → Open Folder as RO-Crate, then open the prepared folder as the RocKIT workspace. When RocKIT reports that ro-crate-metadata.json is missing, choose the option to generate a new RO-Crate metadata file. In the already open RO-Crate Structure Panel, select the root dataset, shown as ./. Associate a metadata profile with the root dataset to determine the editable and required fields. For example, to use ARP's public Citation profile, open Metadata Profile Manager, choose Browse Remote, then select ARP Production → Public → Dataverse → Citation Metadata and download it. Return to the root dataset in the Metadata Editor, choose Add profile, select Citation Metadata, and click Associate. RocKIT stores a local copy, so an already downloaded profile remains available offline. In the Metadata Editor panel, select the associated Citation profile, then add the main dataset metadata: name or title, description, creators, dates, licence, keywords, and other publication fields required by the profile. Review the source files in Workspace and the RO-Crate file and folder entities. If a file is not represented in the crate, drag it from Workspace into the Structure panel or add the relationship from the editor. Add contextual entities such as people, organizations, places, publications, or URLs when a field asks for a linked entity. Open the Entities panel and expand the entities to review them. Open Validation Errors and review the reported problems before they are corrected. Then fix the reported errors. Save the crate. To create an RO-Crate package, run Export RO-Crate; to export the dataset to a data repository, use the repository export workflow. tip For publication, prefer a clean folder structure and meaningful relative file paths before creating the crate.

documents.t: RocKIT can download a dataset from a configured remote repository from File > Repository Operations. Import works with ARP Dataverse, generic Dataverse, and Zenodo repositories. For ARP Dataverse, RocKIT downloads an RO-Crate ZIP; for generic Dataverse, it uses the Dataverse dataset ZIP download; for Zenodo, it downloads the record files and creates RO-Crate metadata. Check that the repository you want to use is configured in Data Repository Manager. Choose File > Repository Operations. In Select Data Repository, click the import (down-arrow) button in the row of the repository you want to use. If the repository is not configured yet, use Add Repository. Enter the dataset URL or persistent identifier to import. For an ARP dataset, use the full handle or dataset URL; for a generic Dataverse dataset, use the persistent identifier or dataset URL; for Zenodo, enter an upload URL in the form https://zenodo.org/uploads/{id}. In Select Import Folder, choose the parent folder where RocKIT should create the new folder for the imported dataset, then click Import Here. Wait while RocKIT downloads and processes the dataset files, then opens the imported folder as the workspace. If the imported package contains ro-crate-metadata.json, continue with the steps for opening and editing an existing RO-Crate. For a Zenodo import, RocKIT creates this file. If a generic Dataverse import does not include RO-Crate metadata, RocKIT can create a new ro-crate-metadata.json after opening the workspace.
documents.s: Quick Start: Import a Dataset from a Remote Repository

documents.t: Open the folder that contains ro-crate-metadata.json. Wait for RocKIT to load the metadata into the application state. Use the RO-Crate Structure to navigate datasets and files. Use Entities when you need to find contextual entities that are not part of the file tree. Select or open an entity to edit it in the Metadata Editor. Save the crate after meaningful changes. Validate the crate in Validation Errors and fix errors before export. If the metadata file is missing, RocKIT offers recovery options for creating a metadata file. If the file exists but cannot be parsed as JSON, RocKIT marks the crate as invalid and opens a recovery dialog. Keep a backup before repairing a crate by hand. Existing ARP Dataverse crates may contain remote-style file identifiers. When RocKIT detects convertible ARP identifiers, it can offer remote-to-local conversion. The conversion changes file and dataset @id values to workspace-relative paths and updates references throughout the metadata. When you save, RocKIT writes the current RO-Crate JSON to ro-crate-metadata.json and regenerates ro-crate-preview.html. For exporting datasets to data repositories, see Repository export and import.

documents.t: By default, RocKIT displays the About RocKIT window when the application starts. The RocKIT Documentation link opens the documentation matching the running application version in your default web browser. The link is highlighted in the screenshot below. If the splash screen is no longer open, select Help > About RocKIT, then select RocKIT Documentation. On the documentation website, use Help in the left navigation to return to this page.

RocKIT uses the standard Theia workbench layout with RO-Crate-specific panels. The main working areas are: Workspace, the standard Theia file explorer for the open folder. RO-Crate Structure, a tree of the root dataset, nested datasets, and files. Metadata Editor, the form-based metadata editor for the selected entity. Entities, a grouped searchable view of all crate entities. Validation Errors, a panel for profile and crate validation messages. Metadata Profile Manager and Data Repository Manager, configuration tools for profile and repository integrations. RO-Crate Preview, a read-only JSON preview of the crate currently held in application state. When a workspace is open, the default layout places Workspace on the left, RO-Crate Structure and Metadata Editor in the main area, and Entities on the right. The main menu includes a dedicated RO-Crate menu. It provides quick access to Workspace, Structure, Metadata Editor, Entities, Validation Errors, Metadata Profile Manager, Data Repository Manager, Preview, Remote to Local Conversion, and Edit with AI Tool. Panels and editors are ordinary Theia widgets. You can close tabs, reopen them from the menu or command palette, resize side panels, and split or move editors using Theia's normal tab controls. If the layout becomes inconvenient, reopen the important RO-Crate views from the RO-Crate menu. The application does not require a specific layout; the panels stay synchronized through the shared RO-Crate application state.

The Entities panel lists RO-Crate entities independently of the file tree. It is useful for people, organizations, URLs, schema-defined objects, and any entity that is hard to find through the dataset hierarchy. Entities are grouped by type. Dataset and File entities also appear here, so the panel can be used as a complete index of the crate.

The Simple search mode provides three filters that are applied together. Entity name performs a case-insensitive partial match against the name shown in the panel; for an unnamed entity, this is its displayed identifier. Validity can show All entities, Only valid, or Only invalid entities. Entity type accepts one or more types present in the current RO-Crate; leaving it empty shows every type. Clear filters restores the simple filters to their defaults. Use the Advanced search mode for compound, property-based conditions. In the Advanced filters dialog, first select an entity type and one or more metadata profiles, and optionally enable properties from other ontologies. You can then create field rules whose available operators adapt to the field's value type, including text matching, null and non-null checks, ranges, and filtering the subfields of objects. Rules can be arranged in nested And, Or, and Not groups. Apply activates the conditions, while Clear filters removes them. Expand or collapse groups to scan large crates more efficiently.

Select an entity to make it the current entity. For detailed editing, double-click the entity: if it is already open in an RO-Crate Editor, RocKIT activates that editor; otherwise, it reuses the most recently used RO-Crate Editor to open the entity. If no RO-Crate Editor is open, RocKIT creates one. To preserve the contents of the existing editor, hold Alt and single-click the entity; it then opens in a new editor tab. Multi-select is available for bulk editing when the selected entities have compatible editable properties.

Deletable entities can be removed from the RO-Crate description. Deleting an entity removes metadata references to it. Be careful with File and Dataset entities, because those entities may also correspond to workspace content or dataset hierarchy links. Note: Operations in the Entities panel, including deletion, do not modify the file system and do not delete directories or files. They only remove the corresponding entities from the RO-Crate description.

Entities with validation errors are marked in the panel. Open the validation dialog or the Validation Errors panel to inspect the full message and navigate to the affected entity. Use Entities when you are working with contextual metadata. Use Structure when the task is about files, folders, or dataset containment.

The Metadata Profile Manager stores metadata profiles that can be associated with RO-Crate entities. Profiles define which metadata fields appear when editing a dataset, file, or other RO-Crate entity, which fields are required, and what kind of values can be entered. Examples include profiles based on the Harvard Dataverse metadata blocks and described in the ARP CEDAR repository; these profiles can be used to describe datasets and data entities. Open it from RO-Crate > Metadata Profile Manager. The manager shows a table of known profiles and a toolbar for profile actions.

Use Import File to import one or more local JSON profile files. Use Import URL to fetch a profile from a URL. Import progress is shown in the workbench, and failed imports remain visible until refreshed or retried. Use Browse Remote to browse templates through a configured remote provider and import them as profiles. Provider configuration is available from the toolbar settings button. A provider configuration contains the provider URL and any required API key or access settings.

A metadata profile provider describes a connection to a remote template repository. RocKIT currently supports CEDAR providers: you can browse their remote templates and import a selected template into the local metadata profile store. RocKIT converts the imported CEDAR template into the profile used by the RO-Crate Editor. On first startup, RocKIT automatically creates the default ARP Production CEDAR profile provider; you can review or modify it in the provider list opened with the Configure Providers icon. To add a provider, open Manage Remote Providers with the toolbar settings button, then select Add Provider. Before saving the provider, RocKIT verifies the connection and adds it to the configuration only after the verification succeeds. The main provider fields are: Name (Display): the name shown in provider lists. Base URL: the URL of the CEDAR interface or service. Type: currently CEDAR. Access: Dataverse proxy (read-only) or CEDAR API key. Dataverse Proxy Base URL: the Dataverse proxy base URL when proxy access is used. API Key: required only for API-key access; RocKIT stores the key in secure storage, not in the provider JSON configuration. The provider referred to later in this documentation as the Default metadata profile provider is the ARP production CEDAR provider. When creating a new provider, the default field values add the ARP Production provider to the system: Field Value Name (Display) ARP Production Base URL https://cedar.schema.researchdata.hu/ Type CEDAR Access Dataverse proxy (read-only) Dataverse Proxy Base URL https://repo.researchdata.hu

If an RO-Crate package references a profile that is not yet available locally, RocKIT attempts to download it. The dataset can be edited only after the profile has been downloaded successfully. Select profiles in the table to delete them. Persisted profiles require confirmation. Profiles waiting to be downloaded or whose download failed can also be removed from the list.

When the Metadata Editor asks for a profile association, select a profile from the profile selector. RocKIT adds the corresponding profile reference to the entity and refreshes the profile-driven editor form. If a crate references a profile that is not available locally, RocKIT can report it as missing. Common problems are invalid JSON, unreachable URLs, provider authentication errors, and profiles that do not define fields in the form expected by RocKIT.

RO-Crate Preview opens a dialog showing the RO-Crate JSON currently held in RocKIT application state. It is useful for reviewing exactly what the editor will save. The preview is a JSON view. It is collapsed by default so you can expand the root, @context, and @graph sections as needed. Use Copy JSON to copy the raw formatted JSON to the clipboard for review, issue reports, or comparison.
The Metadata Editor is the form-based editor for one selected entity. It edits the RO-Crate JSON through structured fields instead of requiring manual JSON editing.

Fields are grouped by the active profile and any metadata profiles associated with the entity. Basic RO-Crate properties appear in the Basic data section: this contains the @id, @type, and Name fields, followed by the profile-specific properties. Required fields are indicated by the form and by validation messages. Entity identifiers are part of the crate's reference structure. Change @id values only when you understand the effect on links. For files and datasets, workspace-relative paths are usually the clearest identifiers in local crates. The editor supports common field types including text, long text, numbers, dates, URLs, booleans, selections, entity references, and map-like values. A field can be added when the schema permits it and removed when the property is optional or repeatable.

The left side of the editor header contains three navigation buttons. The back and forward arrows move through the editor's entity history, and are enabled only when there is a previous or next item in that history. The home icon opens the crate's root entity (./) and is disabled when that entity is already current. The arrow button on the right side of the header opens the linked-entities panel: it lists entities that reference the current entity and opens a selected item in the editor before closing. Many RO-Crate properties refer to another entity rather than storing plain text. For example, an author can be a Person entity reused by several datasets or files. When editing a reference field, choose an existing entity when it already exists, or create a new linked entity when the metadata describes a new person, organization, place, URL, or other contextual object. The editor also exposes reverse relationships: places where the current entity is referenced by other entities. Use those links to move from a person, organization, or URL back to the datasets or files that use it.

The settings button on the right side of the editor header opens the quick filter bar. From this bar you can hide or show field help, hide empty fields, and filter fields by name or current value. When the entity has AI-edited fields, an additional filter button appears so only those fields can be listed. Changes written directly to ro-crate-metadata.json by AI or another external program are also shown on the RO-Crate Editor fields, where they can be accepted, rejected, or manually corrected. The full flow is described in Reviewing external RO-Crate changes.

Traditional profile association uses the + button on the left to add complete profile sections to the entity. Separately, the + Add button in the editor header can add individual metadata fields to the current entity. The + Add button opens a property picker panel. There you can search by name, choose all loaded schemas or one specific schema, then add a schema.org property or a field from another loaded ontology. The Only show matching properties option shows only fields that fit the current entity type by default; when it is turned off, the full property list from the loaded schemas can be browsed. Use the Schemas button to manage the ontologies available in the property picker. In addition to the built-in Schema.org schema, further schemas can be loaded or registered by URL, and you can set which RO-Crate versions they are active for.

Metadata profiles define additional domain- or repository-specific fields beyond the core RO-Crate properties. Use the profile rail on the left side of the editor to select a profile associated with the entity; the selected profile determines which profile-specific fields appear in the form. An entity can have multiple profiles, allowing fields from different schemas to be handled together. Add a new profile to the entity being edited with the + button on the left side of the profile rail. For details about profile availability and configuration, see the Metadata Profile Manager page.

When an AI client or another external tool changes the RO-Crate, the editor marks the affected fields as AI changes that need review. Each suggestion can be accepted or rejected; accepting keeps the externally written value, while rejecting restores the previous value. See Reviewing External RO-Crate Changes for the detailed workflow.

Changes are not persisted to the crate until you perform a save action. Save from the File menu with the Save command, or use the default Ctrl+S keybinding. After saving, the application records RO-Crate changes in history so undo and redo can reverse supported metadata edits during the current session.

The RO-Crate menu groups the main RocKIT views and tools. Menu item Purpose Workspace Opens the workspace file explorer. Structure Opens a new RO-Crate Structure view. Metadata Editor Opens a Metadata Editor widget. Entities Opens the grouped entity browser. Validation Errors Opens the validation errors panel. Metadata Profile Manager Opens the profile import and provider manager. Data Repository Manager Opens repository connection settings. Preview Opens a JSON preview dialog for the current crate. Remote to Local Conversion Converts eligible ARP Dataverse file and dataset identifiers to local workspace-relative identifiers. Edit with AI Tool Opens editing workflows with the available AI assistants. Most menu items have matching command-palette commands. If a panel was closed, using the menu item is the quickest way to recreate it.

The RO-Crate Structure Panel shows the crate as a dataset and file tree. It is the best view for understanding what the root dataset contains and how nested datasets and files are connected. Open the panel with the Structure Panel command in the RO-Crate menu. The root dataset is normally ./. Dataset nodes can be expanded and collapsed. File nodes appear under the dataset that references them through hasPart. Note: Although the contents of the RO-Crate Structure Panel can look like the file system's directory and file structure, changes made here only affect the RO-Crate description. The folders and files in the file system are not modified.

Click an entity to select it. Double-click or use the context menu Edit action to open the entity in the RO-Crate Editor. Multiple selected file or dataset entities can be opened in the multi-entity editor when a bulk edit is useful. The panel supports ordinary multi-selection patterns, including modifier-key selection and range selection (on Windows: Ctrl + click, and Shift + click). The context menu provides two different deletion operations. Delete removes only the hasPart relationship between the selected item and its parent dataset. The entity itself remains in the RO-Crate description; if another dataset also references it, it continues to appear there. If there is no other such relationship, the entity disappears from the Structure panel tree but remains in the RO-Crate description. Delete Entity (Shift+Delete), by contrast, removes the entity from the RO-Crate description and deletes every reference to it. The same operations are available from the keyboard: Delete removes the hasPart relationship, while Shift+Delete deletes the entire entity. Neither operation can delete the root dataset.

Drop files or folders onto a dataset in the Structure panel to add them to the crate. When you drag a new file from the Workspace panel to the Structure panel, RocKIT creates missing metadata entities, adds hasPart references to the target dataset, and gives the dropped files basic technical metadata when it can be computed. Several RO-Crate Structure Panels can be open at the same time, and drag and drop also works between these panels. The default drag-and-drop operation is move. If you hold Alt while dropping, the operation is copy: a new hasPart relationship is created and the old one is not removed.

Entities with validation errors are marked in the tree. Open the validation dialog or the Validation Errors panel to inspect the full message and navigate to the affected entity. Use the Structure panel for file hierarchy work: adding payload files, reviewing nested datasets, opening file metadata, and finding where validation errors occur in the dataset tree.

Eclipse Theia is an open-source framework: a shared foundation for applications with different purposes. RocKIT uses this foundation for its workspace and adds tools for managing RO-Crate data packages and research metadata. For a data steward, Theia mainly helps bring files, the structure of a data package, and metadata together in one manageable interface. Theia provides the general parts of the workspace: menus, a file explorer for the open folder, editor tabs, and panels that you can rearrange. For example, you can keep the files in a data package alongside an entity's metadata and adjust panel widths to suit your task. The command palette lets you find and run commands by name; see the Command Reference for how to use it. RocKIT's own features build on this shared workspace: displaying the RO-Crate structure, editing entities and their metadata, managing profiles, and reviewing validation errors. In this documentation, “Theia” generally refers to the application's common controls, while descriptions of the RO-Crate panels explain data stewardship tasks. You do not need programming knowledge or a separate Theia installation to use RocKIT. Theia can also be enhanced with plugins, often called extensions, which add tools and features to the workspace. You can browse available extensions in the Open VSX Registry. Whether extensions can be installed and work as expected depends on the settings and version of the Theia-based application; not every item in the catalogue will necessarily work in RocKIT. You can learn more about the project on the official Theia website. The Theia IDE presented there is an application for programmers built on the same framework; follow this documentation for the tools available in RocKIT. The next page, Application Layout, shows where to find the panels you need for your work.

The Workspace panel is Theia's standard file explorer for the open folder. It shows physical files and folders from the root of the data package opened for editing. In contrast, the RO-Crate Structure Panel, RO-Crate Editor, and Entities Panel show metadata entities loaded from ro-crate-metadata.json: the metadata description and the physical files in an RO-Crate data package may differ. To describe a file as part of the data package, it must appear as a File entity and be connected—usually through a hasPart relationship—to a Dataset entity. A file-system folder normally corresponds to a Dataset entity in the RO-Crate description, so folders may be represented as datasets. When a new RO-Crate is created within an existing file structure (see Quick Start: Create an RO-Crate from Scratch), the application automatically creates the Dataset and File hierarchy from that structure, adding every file and directory in the open folder to the description. If the physical file structure changes later—for example, a file is created, deleted, moved, or its contents change—the application helps detect the change, but it is added to the description only with user involvement.

You can add new files to the workspace by copying them into the data package's source directory with your operating system's file manager. You can also drag files or folders from the operating system's file manager directly into RocKIT's Workspace panel; the application then copies them into the workspace.

RocKIT automatically compares the files in the workspace with the contents of ro-crate-metadata.json. The Workspace panel highlights files that are not yet included in the RO-Crate description, making new or undescribed files easy to identify. Drag highlighted files or folders from the Workspace panel onto the appropriate data package in the RO-Crate Structure Panel. RocKIT creates the missing File or Dataset entities, adds them to the target data package, and, when a file can be read, records useful metadata such as its name, MIME type, and file size. After a file has been added successfully, its highlight disappears.
documents.s: Adding Files to the RO-Crate Description

documents.t: Click the magnifying-glass icon in the Workspace panel toolbar to display the search and filter fields. Enter text in the File name field to narrow the file list. The RO-Crate descriptions filter can show all files, only files with a description, or only files that are not yet included in the RO-Crate description. Select Clear filters to restore the complete list.

You can associate an external directory with the workspace by selecting Add New Data Source. The associated directory and its files appear in the Workspace panel, from where you can drag files into the RO-Crate Structure Panel to add them to the RO-Crate description. External directories do not become part of the RO-Crate's physical file hierarchy; several different ro-crate-metadata.json descriptions can refer to the same external directory. When exporting, RocKIT includes only those external files that are present in the current RO-Crate description.

RocKIT creates or uses: ro-crate-metadata.json ro-crate-preview.html .rockit/ .rockit/ignored.txt The .rockit directory is reserved for RocKIT technical data. Its contents are not part of the data package and should not be described as RO-Crate content files. Depending on the workflows used in the application, additional technical files may appear there. The .rockit/ignored.txt file contains ignore rules. Ignore rules prevent technical or unwanted files from being included in exports. Default rules are added when RocKIT saves ignore settings. Clean exports also omit RocKIT technical files and package only crate-relevant content. You can also manage the ignore rules from the Workspace panel's context menu. Right-click a file or folder and select Omit from RO-Crate Description. RocKIT adds the item's path to the ignore rules and, if it already has a corresponding File or Dataset entity, removes its description from the RO-Crate. The item is then excluded from exports. To allow an omitted file or folder again, select Include in RO-Crate Description from its context menu. This removes the effect of the applicable ignore rule, making the item eligible for export again. The command does not create a metadata entity by itself; to describe the item as part of the RO-Crate, drag it to the RO-Crate Structure Panel as explained above.

The Data Repository Manager stores connection settings for remote repositories used by repository-oriented workflows. RocKIT recognizes ARP Data Repository, generic Dataverse repositories, and Zenodo; the ARP Data Repository workflow has the most complete support. Open it from RO-Crate > Data Repository Manager. The table lists configured repositories. Use Add Repository to create a configuration, and use row actions to edit or delete existing entries. Multiple selected repositories can be deleted after confirmation.

The repository dialog requires: Display name. Base URL, using http or https. API token. RocKIT uses the supplied URL to detect whether the service is ARP Data Repository, generic Dataverse, Zenodo, or an unsupported repository. When you save, RocKIT tests the connection by calling the Dataverse token endpoint with the provided token. If the server returns token information, the dialog shows a success confirmation and stores the configuration. Invalid URLs, network failures, non-JSON responses, and rejected tokens are shown as errors. When editing an existing repository, the stored API token is hidden. Choose Change if you need to replace it. The toolbar's Import and Export buttons start remote repository workflows. Import downloads a remote dataset and opens it as a new local workspace. Export can create a remote dataset or update an existing target recorded in the export log. See Repository export and import for details.

Saving and exporting are separate actions. Save RO-Crate writes the current metadata to ro-crate-metadata.json in the workspace root and regenerates ro-crate-preview.html. It also persists RocKIT ignore rules in .rockit/ignored.txt when ignore rules are available. Use File > Package RO-Crate to create a ZIP package from the open workspace. In the dialog, select the package type, choose whether external files should be included, then click Package and select the destination of the ZIP file. Packaging cannot start while the RO-Crate metadata contains unsaved changes. Use Save in the dialog to save them; after a successful save, the Package button becomes available.

Normal Package adds the complete workspace to the ZIP, except for items excluded by ignore rules. It always includes ro-crate-metadata.json and ro-crate-preview.html, even if an ignore rule would otherwise exclude them. Its default filename is <workspace>.zip. Clean RO-Crate Package contains ro-crate-metadata.json, the existing ro-crate-preview.html, and available workspace files referenced as files by the metadata. Other workspace files and RocKIT technical files are omitted. This mode requires a ro-crate-metadata.json file that RocKIT can parse successfully. Its default filename is <workspace>-clean.zip.

Include referenced local files that are outside the RO-Crate folder is cleared by default. When selected, RocKIT looks for locally resolvable files referenced by the RO-Crate metadata but stored outside the workspace folder and adds copies to the ZIP. These files are placed under imported_resources; if names collide, RocKIT selects a unique directory or filename. The option applies only to readable files referenced by the metadata: it does not add arbitrary external files, directories, or unresolved references. When the checkbox is cleared, local files outside the workspace are not included. The option is available for both normal and clean packages.

RocKIT reads ignore rules from .rockit/ignored.txt and combines them with default ignored entries. Rules are normalized to workspace-relative paths. Negated rules can re-include a path. Ignore rules apply to both package types. After packaging, inspect the ZIP before uploading or distributing it. Check that ro-crate-metadata.json and the expected payload files are present and, when external files were included, inspect the contents of imported_resources.

Remote-to-local conversion is for ARP Data Repository RO-Crates whose file and dataset entities use ARP remote identifiers such as https://w3id.org/arp/ro-id/.../file/.... Local editing and export are easier when those entities use workspace-relative paths. The conversion command: Saves open files. Reads ro-crate-metadata.json from the workspace root. Checks that the root dataset has an @arpPid. Finds File and Dataset entities with ARP remote identifiers. Derives a local path from directoryLabel and name. Replaces entity @id values and updates @id references throughout the JSON. Moves old File identifiers into url; Dataset identifiers are not moved into url. Writes the converted metadata back to ro-crate-metadata.json. The command stops if it cannot create unique local paths. It also skips entities that are not File or Dataset entities, are missing identifiers, are not ARP-local identifiers, or do not contain enough path metadata. Review the Structure panel and Preview after conversion. Then validate the crate and save a backup if the converted identifiers are correct.

RocKIT can import RO-Crate workspaces from remote repositories, export new datasets, and link, update, or synchronize local and remote copies. These operations are not available directly from the File menu. Open RO-Crate > Repository Operations to display the Select Data Repository window. Repository workflows use configurations stored in the Data Repository Manager. A repository's base URL and API token can be entered beforehand in the manager or directly in the Repository Operations window.

ARP Data Repository: supports the ARP RO-Crate ZIP upload endpoint and the native Dataverse API. This is the best-supported workflow. Generic Dataverse repositories: partially supported through the native Dataverse API. Zenodo: partially supported through the Zenodo API.

The window shows every configured repository and any remote export targets previously recorded for the current workspace. The following functions can be initiated here: Import from remote: downloads a remote dataset and opens it as a new local workspace. An existing open workspace is not required. New export: creates a new remote dataset or Zenodo deposition from the open local RO-Crate. Upload updates: updates the metadata and files of a previously recorded remote target from the local workspace. Sync from remote: applies the remote dataset's metadata and new or changed files to an already linked local workspace. Three modes are available: Complete sync: uses the remote metadata and structure. Download remote additions: preserves local edits and adds remote-only entities and relationships. Keep only local additions: uses the remote version as the base, then restores local-only entities and relationships. Link to remote: associates the open local RO-Crate with an existing remote dataset. It does not upload or download data; it records the relationship and entity mappings under .rockit/ for later updates and synchronization. Unlink: removes the local link and mapping while leaving the remote dataset unchanged. Delete: removes the remote Dataverse draft or Zenodo deposition, then removes the local link. A published Dataverse dataset normally cannot be deleted; usually only its latest draft can be removed. Add and edit repositories: creates a repository configuration or changes an existing one. New export, upload updates, synchronization, and linking require an open workspace. For a failed or cancelled export, error details can also be opened from this window.
documents.s: Functions in the Repository Operations window

documents.t: In Select Data Repository, click Import from remote for the required repository. Enter the dataset URL, handle, DOI, or persistent identifier. Select the local folder where RocKIT should create the imported workspace. RocKIT downloads the dataset and opens the resulting directory as the active workspace. For Dataverse repositories, RocKIT downloads the dataset ZIP through the access API. If it contains ro-crate-metadata.json, the folder can be opened as an RO-Crate workspace immediately. Otherwise, RocKIT still imports the files and metadata can be created later. The ARP dialog accepts a dataset handle or URL. For Zenodo imports, RocKIT downloads the record's files and creates RO-Crate metadata for them.

In Select Data Repository, click New export on a repository row to create a remote dataset. Click Upload updates for a previous export target listed below the repository to update that same remote dataset. Save the RO-Crate before exporting. Remote export is blocked while the in-memory RO-Crate has unsaved changes. RocKIT also calculates and stores checksums so that it can compare the local workspace with a previously uploaded dataset. As a minimum requirement, associate the Citation profile from the default metadata profile provider with the root Dataset entity, then complete Author, Point of Contact, and Subject. See Metadata Profile Providers for provider setup. For ARP Data Repository, RocKIT creates an RO-Crate ZIP and uploads it through the ARP endpoint. For a generic Dataverse repository, it uses the native Dataverse API, asks for citation metadata required by that installation, creates a draft, and uploads the files. On Zenodo it creates a new deposition. When updating an existing export, RocKIT uploads new or changed files, removes files that are no longer required, and updates supported metadata.

Start synchronization from Sync options on a recorded export target. Remote metadata is applied to the local RO-Crate using the selected crosswalk file, and new or changed remote files are downloaded. Files deleted remotely remain on disk but may become orphaned. Because synchronization can overwrite local data, save or archive any version that must be retained before starting it. Use Link to remote when the same dataset already exists both locally and in a repository but RocKIT has not yet recorded their relationship. Enter the remote dataset PID or URL. RocKIT checks the remote dataset, warns if its title differs, and then creates the mapping file. If an entity identifier cannot be mapped, RocKIT records an empty value and reports the affected identifiers.

After an import or synchronization, inspect the workspace and its ro-crate-metadata.json. After an export or update, review the repository dataset page and RocKIT warnings. If unmapped entity identifiers are reported, inspect the mapping file under .rockit/.

Start with a clean folder structure. Rename files and organize folders before creating final metadata so entity identifiers can stay stable. Describe the root dataset first. Add a clear title or name, description, creators, licence, dates, keywords, and repository-required fields before spending time on detailed file metadata. Use stable identifiers. For local crates, workspace-relative file paths are easier to review and export than temporary absolute paths. Avoid changing @id values late unless you are intentionally repairing identifiers. Reuse contextual entities. Create one Person or Organization entity and link to it from multiple datasets or files instead of creating near-duplicates. Use metadata profiles when the project needs domain-specific fields. Associate profiles deliberately and remove unused profiles before publication. Validate early and often. Validation errors are easier to fix while you still remember the edit that caused them. Preview before saving and exporting. Check the @graph, hasPart hierarchy, conformsTo values, and references to people, organizations, URLs, and files. Use clean export for publication. Keep backups or version-control copies of important ro-crate-metadata.json files.

RocKIT commands are available from menus and the Theia Command Palette. Open the palette from View > Command Palette… or with its keyboard shortcut. See RO-Crate Menu Reference for the structure of the RO-Crate menu.

Command Purpose Open Folder as RO-Crate Opens a folder as the workspace. If it has no ro-crate-metadata.json, RocKIT offers to initialize the RO-Crate. Open Recent RO-Crate Opens a previously used RO-Crate workspace. Close RO-Crate Closes the current workspace and offers to save unsaved changes. Save RO-Crate Saves metadata to ro-crate-metadata.json, the preview to ro-crate-preview.html, and ignore rules to .rockit/ignored.txt. Revert to Saved RO-Crate Discards unsaved metadata changes and reloads the RO-Crate stored on disk. Package RO-Crate Opens the packaging dialog, where a normal or clean ZIP package can be created.

Command or menu item Purpose Workspace Shows or hides the workspace file explorer. Structure Panel Opens the hierarchical RO-Crate structure view. Its related Command Palette command is Open New RO-Crate Structure. Metadata Editor Opens a metadata editor for the selected entity. Its related Command Palette command is Open New Metadata Editor. Entities Opens the searchable, filterable, grouped entity view, from which Multi Edit can also be started. Validation Errors Opens the current RO-Crate validation errors panel. Metadata Profile Manager Opens management for installed and pending metadata profiles and profile providers. Data Repository Manager Opens connection settings for remote data repositories. Global Entity Library Opens the store of global entities that can be reused across RO-Crates. Preview Opens a JSON preview of the current in-memory RO-Crate. Remote to Local Conversion Converts eligible ARP repository file and dataset identifiers to local workspace-relative identifiers. Repository Operations Opens the window for repository import, new export, update, synchronization, linking, and link management. Edit with AI Tool Opens editing options provided by configured AI assistants.

Command Purpose Undo and Redo Reverses or reapplies supported RO-Crate metadata changes. Multi Edit Applies the same field operation to selected items from the Entities view. Initialize RO-Crate Creates initial RO-Crate metadata for the open workspace. The Command Palette is especially useful when a panel is closed or hidden. Search using the command label in the interface's current language; useful terms include “RO-Crate”, “profile”, “repository”, “preview”, and “validation”.

ro-crate-metadata.json is the primary RO-Crate metadata file. RocKIT loads it from the workspace root and saves edited metadata back to it. ro-crate-preview.html is regenerated when the crate is saved. It is a human-readable preview artifact and can be included in normal exports. .rockit/ stores RocKIT-specific workspace files. The most important one is .rockit/ignored.txt, which contains ignore rules used by save and export workflows. RocKIT may also use an RO-Crate approval file to track external metadata changes, profile storage and indexes for imported metadata profiles, remote profile provider configuration, data repository configuration, and secure credential storage for tokens or API keys. The application-level profile store uses metadata-profile-index.json, the metadata-profiles/cedar/ and metadata-profiles/ro-crate/ directories, and the remote-profile-providers.json provider configuration by default. Do not edit application configuration or credential storage files manually unless you are repairing a known issue. Manual edits to ro-crate-metadata.json are possible, but the file must remain valid JSON and should be reloaded and validated in RocKIT afterwards.
documents.s: Files Created or Used by RocKIT

documents.t: RocKIT uses standard Theia keyboard and mouse behavior where possible. Action Interaction Open command palette Use the standard Theia command-palette shortcut for your platform. Save Use the standard save shortcut while an RO-Crate editor or file editor is focused. Select one entity Click the entity in Structure or Entities. Multi-select Use Ctrl or Cmd with clicks, depending on platform. Range select Use Shift selection where the tree or table supports it. Open entity Double-click or use the context menu edit action. Delete selected entities Press Delete when focus is in an RO-Crate panel and the selection is deletable. Add files Drag files or folders into the Structure panel. Copy preview JSON Use Copy JSON in RO-Crate Preview. Copy chat transcript Use the transcript copy action in the AI assistant chat. Delete is ignored while focus is inside text inputs, text areas, editable content, or text boxes, so normal text editing remains safe.

Check that the workspace root contains ro-crate-metadata.json and that the file is valid JSON. If the crate uses ARP remote identifiers, accept conversion only after confirming that the workspace contains the corresponding files.
The Structure panel follows dataset hasPart relationships. A File or Dataset entity can exist in @graph but not appear in the tree if no visible dataset references it.
documents.s: An entity is missing from Structure

documents.t: Drop onto a dataset node, not an empty area. Confirm the file is readable and that the workspace is open. If the file is outside the workspace, check whether the resulting absolute identifier is acceptable for your workflow.
documents.s: Drag and Drop Does Not Add a File

documents.t: Refresh the Metadata Profile Manager. If the import failed, inspect the error, fix the profile file or URL, and retry.
Verify the base URL, token value, repository type, and network access. For ARP Dataverse, the token test calls the Dataverse token endpoint.
Save or refresh validation, then open the entity named by the error. Also check linked entities and missing profiles, because the visible field may only be the reference that exposes the problem.
Check .rockit/ignored.txt, clean export rules, and whether the files are actually referenced by the crate metadata.
Check the native agent provider setup, RO-Crate MCP daemon startup, workspace permissions, and provider credentials.

When RocKIT cannot load the crate, it tries to keep the workspace open and show a recovery path. If ro-crate-metadata.json is missing, use the recovery dialog to create a new metadata file for the workspace. If the file exists but is invalid JSON, repair it from a backup or use the recovery option only when you are comfortable replacing the current metadata. File read and write errors usually mean the workspace or export destination is not writable, the file is locked by another process, or the path is no longer available. Check permissions and save again. Profile import errors can be caused by invalid JSON, an unsupported profile shape, unreachable URLs, or remote provider authentication problems. Retry after fixing the source or provider configuration. Repository connection errors are reported during repository save because RocKIT tests the token against the repository. Confirm the base URL, token, and network access. Export errors usually come from unreadable files, unwritable ZIP destinations, or unsaved metadata. Save first, then retry export to a simple local path. When reporting a problem, include the workflow, the error text, whether the crate was new or existing, and a minimized ro-crate-metadata.json when possible.
Yes, but the file must remain valid JSON and valid RO-Crate metadata. Reload and validate it in RocKIT afterwards.
The file system changes, but metadata identifiers and references may still use the old path. Update the crate metadata and validate.
